10611-an-essay-on-the-slavery-and-commer:
Thomas Clarkson wrote this essay in Latin as a Cambridge student, won the university's first prize for it in 1785, and published it in English in 1786. It attacks the African slave trade and the commerce built on enslaved labor, arguing from reason, history, and humanity. Clarkson dedicated it to the Earl of Portmore and addressed it to readers already debating freedom.

The essay traces how people were seized, sold, and held, and answers the defenses offered for the trade. Its plain, forceful case helped launch Clarkson's lifelong campaign against slavery. Readers meet a founding text of British abolition, written by a young man who would spend his life on the cause.
12883-by-the-golden-gate-or-san-francisc:
Joseph Carey's By the Golden Gate, published in 1902, presents San Francisco as queen city of the Pacific coast. Chapters travel westward, view the bay by boat, retell the gold discovery, and tour Golden Gate Park, cemeteries, street names, Chinatown, music halls, gambling, and the joss-house. The General Convention of 1901 gets its own chapter.

A prison visit shows Carey's moral eye: an old offender with a face furrowed by sin regards visitors as intruders, while the writer recalls Watts on sinners hardened in crime. Carey writes as a clergyman and historian. The book gives a vivid, period portrait of San Francisco at the turn of the century.
16639-the-fotygraft-album-shown-to-the-n:
Frank Wing draws and writes this 1915 picture book as Rebecca Sparks Peters, aged eleven, showing the family album to a new neighbor, Mrs. Miggs. Ma has run to borrow thread, molasses, and eggs, so Rebecca settles Mrs. Miggs on the sofa and begins: this first one is ma when she was little, cute in furs her Uncle Seth gave her from his Davenport store.

The humor lies in a child's voice and a child's eye for family history. Wing's drawings match the talk, homely and funny. Readers of American humor will find a charming period piece, warm with small-town neighborliness.
17681-lippa:
Beatrice Egerton wrote this novel, published in London by Eden, Remington and Company of King Street, Covent Garden. Its first chapter opens with a Shakespeare motto on the world as a stage where every man must play a part. At four o'clock on a July day, a London street wears a deserted look. Cab drivers doze in attitudes far from comfort, and sentries at a palace look almost suffocated in their bearskins.

Readers get a late Victorian society novel, opening in summer heat and theatrical metaphor. The book suits readers of forgotten women novelists of the 1890s and of London social fiction. Its transcriber notes that chapter numbering follows the original, with two chapter elevens.
20503-the-nation-s-river-a-report-on-the:
The Nation's River is a United States Department of the Interior report on the Potomac River. The Potomac flows past the capital, and the report treats it as a national trust. It studies the river's pollution, banks, and public use.

To protect the mainstem Potomac and its banks from Washington to Cumberland, Maryland, the report urges quick action. It calls for legislative authorization, funding, and a Potomac national river area open to the public. The report shows the conservation thinking of its time: a great river near a great city should belong to everyone.
20629-torchy-as-a-pa:
Torchy as a Pa, published in 1919, makes Sewell Ford's slangy hero a father. Torchy greets fatherhood the way he greeted office work: fast talk first, feelings after. A card announcing the new arrival sets the comedy going.

He picks the card on the fly and reads the neat script on it. At home after September 15, it says, at an address on West Hundred and Umpty-Umpt Street. Hamilton Porter Blake, anyway? Torchy demands, missing the point as usual. The book follows him through babies, in-laws, and the Corrugated Trust, in the series' longest-running vein of fun.
21499-europe-whither-bound-quo-vadis-eur:
Stephen Graham asks where Europe is heading in Europe, Whither Bound?, letters from the capitals of 1921. The book came out in 1922, after the letters ran in Country Life. Graham made no deep study of each land; he kept the taxi waiting, as he jokes.

That speed is the point: he wanted Europe seen whole, as one body. Pride of Christian culture before 1914 now faced, he feared, decline and death. Bishops, editors, and officers helped him on his rapid tour. Few travel books so soon after the Great War tried to grasp the continent entire.
2273-tom-swift-and-his-motor-boat-or-the:
Victor Appleton's young inventor Tom Swift turns his genius to a fast motor boat, and rivals on Lake Carlopa will stop at nothing to beat or steal it. Tom Swift and His Motor Boat mixes races, chases, and a mystery about a stolen boat design, with Tom's friends Ned and Mr. Damon along for the ride. The inventions are explained just enough to feel real.

The story moves briskly from workshop to water, with danger arriving at every regatta. Boys of its era thrilled to Tom's pluck and machinery, and the series launched a long line of young inventor heroes. Modern readers get a lively window into early twentieth century adventure fiction.
23072-the-voyage-of-the-steadfast-the-yo:
W. H. G. Kingston sounds a wreck alarm in The Voyage of the Steadfast. Hannah cries out at a gun flash near the dark rocks offshore. A second flash follows. Some unfortunate ship, she is sure, is signaling from the reef, perhaps already wrecked on it.

The Steadfast carries young missionaries toward the Pacific, and storm, wreck, and rescue test their calling early. Kingston wrote sea adventure with a missionary heart, filling the Pacific with converts, dangers, and providence. His books shaped British boys' picture of the ocean world. This voyage shows his whole method, a gun flash in the dark, a boat launched into surf, and faith keeping stroke with the oars.
25477-the-curlytops-on-star-island-or-ca:
Howard R. Garis sends Ted and Jan Martin, the Curlytops, camping on Star Island with Grandpa Martin. Ted, whose full name is Theodore Baradale Martin, teases his sister Janet until their mother calls them in. Chapters follow a blue light, a farmer's tale, a trip to the island, and a fall overboard. A bag of salt, a bear, a grapevine swing, and a cake made by Trouble fill the holiday.

Ted finds a cave and follows a path from the spring, calling Jan to hurry as his voice fades like a boy gone down a cellar. The children hunt for a tramp's hiding place and dig for gold on the island. Cupples and Leon published the book in New York in 1918, illustrated by Julia Greene.
25488-the-grocery-man-and-peck-s-bad-boy:
George W. Peck's second Bad Boy book pits a mischievous boy against his pa and the grocery man. Chapter headings promise variegated dogs dyed pink, blue, green, and white, a boy sleeping on the roof, and a father wanting polynurious water. The magic bouquet causes a fight at church, a boom in liniment follows, and mining stock mania sweeps deacons and hired girls alike.

Later chapters bring a stabbing, a burglary, dynamite and a Fenian scare in Milwaukee, and pa as an Orangeman. The bad boy narrates in slang, always one prank ahead of his father's temper. Peck published the sketches in 1883, as Peck's Bad Boy and His Pa, number two, with the grocery man taking his turn at the boy's jokes.
25970-a-full-description-of-the-great-to:
Richard Darlington Jr., principal of Ercildoun Seminary, gives a full account of the great tornado that struck western Chester County, Pennsylvania, on July 1, 1877. Printed at West Chester, the pamphlet answers a public wish for the storm's movement, conduct, and origin, with such scientific explanation as may throw light on the marvel. Darlington studied the track for weeks after the storm.

The loss was vast: Phipps and Shields each lost about twelve hundred dollars, and some thirty acres of timber fell on their lands and Joseph Brinton's to the southeast. One life was lost, a woman caught between joists and rafters, while children near her escaped unhurt. The wind cloud veered about eight degrees north after striking the forest tract. The pamphlet is a careful local record of ruin and narrow escapes.
27910-under-the-ensign-of-the-rising-sun:
Harry Collingwood wrote Under the Ensign of the Rising Sun, a story of the Russo-Japanese war, opening with Paul Swinburne dismissed from the navy at seventeen and a half. After heading the Dartmouth passing-out list and serving well for three and a half years, Swinburne was court-martialed through the machinations of his cousin Bob Carr.

Parting from his friend Ronald Gordon at Portland station, Swinburne heads for London to seek his fortune. The story follows him to service under the Japanese flag. The novel mixes naval adventure with a wronged hero's vindication, in Collingwood's vigorous seafaring style.
3025-a-mountain-europa:
John Fox Junior wrote A Mountain Europa as a short novel of the Kentucky mountains, first in his series of mountain stories. The story centers on a cabin gray and tottering with age, guarded like a fortress, with one way of approach straight to the porch. Vines creep from a cliff to roof and chimney, waving tendrils about a thin blue spiral of smoke.

Above the porch, apple branches hold leaves matching the moss on rough shingles, while an old woman spins below and a hound sleeps. Fox's mountain heroine, Europa, bridges the world of the cabin and the world beyond. The tale charms as a brief, atmospheric romance of Appalachia, written with Fox's ear for place and speech.
30588-the-pony-rider-boys-in-alaska-or-t:
Frank Gee Patchin writes The Pony Rider Boys in Alaska, subtitled The Gold Diggers of Taku Pass, copyrighted in 1924 by the Saalfield Publishing Company. Patchin, author of many Pony Rider Boys books from the Rockies and Texas to Montana, the Ozarks, New Mexico, and the Grand Canyon, sends his boys north in this volume.

A frontispiece shows Tad shouting, I file the claim, and contents open with Through Enchanting Waters and the mystery of the gold diggers. Alaska's passes, claims, and rival prospectors drive the plot. Patchin writes a brisk boys' adventure of horses, gold, and northern wilds, in a long, popular series for young readers.
31760-why-do-we-need-a-public-library-ma:
Compiled by Chalmers Hadley, secretary of the American Library Association, this 1910 tract gathers material for a campaign to found a public library. Issued as Library Tract Number 10, it argues the case for a town library and supplies the arguments, lists, and examples a local committee would need.

The volume also catalogs the association's own publications, from reference guides and reading lists to catalog rules and children's books. Readers get a practical piece of library history: not a story, but the working kit behind the spread of free public libraries in American towns.
5989-the-curlytops-on-star-island-or-cam:
Howard R. Garis sends the Curlytop children camping on Star Island with Grandpa. The chapters open with a blue light and a farmer's tale, then an overboard scare, a bag of salt, Ted and the bear, and Jan seeing something strange. Trouble, the youngest, keeps stirring things up.

Caves, a grapevine swing, swimming, digging for gold, and a big hole follow, with trouble making a cake and a playhouse along the way. The book closes with the blue light again and a happy tramp home. Garis keeps the fun brisk, outdoor, and safe for small readers.
a-mountain-europa:
John Fox Jr. sets his tale in the high Kentucky Cumberlands, the country of his famous feud stories. A young woman of the mountains, Europa, grows up where family honor is guarded with rifles and where a stranger from the lowlands is watched with suspicion. Her beauty and spirit draw notice beyond her valley.

Fox follows her through the pressures of mountain custom, courtship, and the old quarrels that rule men's lives around her. He writes the ridges, coves, and fiddle music of the region with the affection that made him the Cumberlands' best-known novelist. The story is a romance, but its weight lies in showing how completely the mountains shape the people born among them.
an-essay-on-the-slavery-and-commerce-of-: Thomas Clarkson writes an essay on the slavery and commerce of the human species, particularly the African. Translated from a Latin dissertation, it won the first prize at Cambridge in 1785, with additions. The work argues against the slave trade on grounds of justice and humanity, drawing on ancient and modern sources. Clarkson's essay helped launch the British campaign that would end the trade.
britannica-1911-agrippa:
Agrippa, the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, was a sceptical philosopher of ancient Greece. His dates cannot be fixed, though he lived later than Aenesidemus, a thinker usually placed near Cicero's time. To Agrippa are credited the five tropes, or lines of argument, summed up by Sextus Empiricus for the later sceptics.

One trope stresses that philosophers disagree on every basic point, so neither sense nor reason can be trusted alone. A second shows proof needing proof without end. Others note that sense data shift with the perceiver, that knowledge rests on unproved assumptions, and that proving sense by reason and reason by sense moves in a circle. The wise course, the tropes conclude, is to affirm nothing and deny nothing.
britannica-1911-ballston-spa:
Ballston Spa was a village and the county seat of Saratoga county, New York, about seven miles south of Saratoga Springs. Its population grew from 3,527 in 1890 to 4,138 in the census of 1910. Rail and electric lines linked it with Saratoga Springs, Albany, and Schenectady.

Paper-bag making, among the largest works of its kind in the country, and a big tannery led its industry. Yet the village was best known as a summer resort. The 1911 Britannica entry describes springs rising through solid rock from about 650 feet, giving fizzy water valued for health and for sale. The village was named for the Reverend Eliphalet Ball, an early settler.
by-the-golden-gate-or-san-francisco-the-:
Joseph Carey wrote a portrait of San Francisco, dated 1902. Its full title calls the city queen of the Pacific coast, with scenes of its life. Carey held a doctor of divinity and sat in the American Historical Association. His wife gets the book in warm words. Westward travel opens the frame.

Views from the bay boat come next. Gold's find and the city's birth fill the third place. Golden Gate Park and the graves get a tale of their own. Then and now — 1849 set by 1901 — gives the growth test. Street names to a cannon fill one wide sweep. Chinese life takes three full parts: work and ways, a press and an opium joint, and the joss house with faith and law. Music, gambling, food, and stage life fill the gay side.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrogio-fopp:
Ambrogio Foppa, generally called Caradosso, was an Italian goldsmith, sculptor, and die sinker, born at Mondonico near Como, or Pavia by other accounts, in 1445. He died about 1527. His Christian name may have been Cristoforo, not Ambrogio. He served Lodovico il Moro of Milan, making a fine medal and goldsmith's pieces, then worked in Rome for Julius II and Leo X.

Cellini called him the most excellent goldsmith of his time, without equal in dies, citing his Rome medal showing Bramante and his St. Peter's design. He is credited with San Satiro's sacristy terra-cotta reliefs, nearly Donatello's equal in beauty, and with medals of Julius II, Francesco Sforza, and Gian Giacomo Trivulzio. Many Italian church sacristies hold goldsmith work attributed to him, especially reliquaries, morses, and crosiers, plus a papal mitre for Julius II.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arequipa:
Arequipa, suffragan of the archdiocese of Lima in Peru, was erected by Gregory XIII on 15 April 1577 at Philip II's request. Philip had sought three Peruvian dioceses under royal patronage. Its population in 1901 was 35,000, and it holds a cathedral honouring the Assumption of the Virgin, a Jesuit college, an infirmary, and several convents. Arequipa is Peru's second city, near the volcanic Andean peak called Misti.

In 1868 earthquake shocks destroyed most of its buildings and killed 6,000 people. The city was founded by Pizarro. The entry is a compact diocesan sketch, joining church institutions to civic disaster. It shows a colonial foundation, a cathedral city under a volcano, and a community rebuilt after a quake that levelled most of what it had built.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atahuallpa:
Atahuallpa, properly Atau-Huallpa, a name usually derived from huallpa, some native bird, was son of the Inca war leader Huayna Capac and a woman from Quito. Hence, descent running in the female line, he was not an Inca but an Indian of Ecuador. Long wars in which Incas overpowered Ecuadorian tribes brought permanent Inca war parties to Ecuador, mixing Inca men with Quito women and children into a new tribe.

Collisions followed between that tribe and descendants of Inca women, with Atau-Huallpa leading the former and Huascar, duly elected war chief at Cuzco, leading the latter. Atau-Huallpa behaved with great cruelty, nearly exterminating resisting Ecuadorian tribes, finally prevailed, and sent warriors south along the mountain spine against Cuzco. When Pizarro landed at Tumbez on Peru's northern coast in 1532, the Quito-Cuzco struggle shaped the conquest that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chilapa: A short entry on the Diocese of Chilapa in Mexico, suffragan to the Archdiocese of Mexico and covering the southern state of Guerrero. Created in 1863, it has had three bishops: Ambrosio Serrano, Ramon Ibarra, and Homobono Anaya. Its population, counted as entirely Catholic, stands at 361,239 souls, served by 64 parishes and 94 priests. Chilapa, the episcopal city, lies about 125 miles south-west of Mexico City and held 8,256 people in 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clemens-non-p:
Clemens non Papa, whose true name was Jacques Clement, represented the sixteenth-century Flemish or Netherland school of music and died in 1558. The one certain fact of his life: he preceded Nicolas Gombert as Charles the Fifth's court choirmaster. His nickname non Papa means not the Pope. It distinguished him from the contemporary Pope Clement the Seventh, who reigned from 1523 to 1534.

His style stays always noble and fluent. Yet he shows his school's fault: contrapuntal forms elaborated at clear declamation's expense. Nevertheless he ranks among Palestrina's and Orlandus Lassus's chief forerunners, overshadowed by them alone. His more important works include ten masses, for six, five, and four voices, published at Louvain from 1555 to 1580. They also include many motets and four volumes of Souter Liedekens, psalms set to familiar Netherland melodies, published at Antwerp in 1556 to 1557.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-auri:
Giovanni Aurispa was a famous Italian humanist and collector of Greek manuscripts, born about 1369 at Noto in Sicily, who died at Ferrara in 1459. In 1418 he went to Constantinople to learn Greek and gather codices, working so hard that he was accused of stripping the city of books. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar whose haul reshaped the West's Greek library.

He returned to Venice in 1423 with 238 volumes of classical authors. Among them were a tenth-century codex of Sophocles and Aeschylus, plus Homer, Demosthenes, Plato, and Xenophon. He then taught Greek at Bologna and Florence, and later served as secretary to Eugene IV in 1441 and to Nicholas V six years later. Besides collecting, he wrote letters, epigrams, and an elegy of some merit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hypaepa:
Hypaepa was a titular see of Asia Minor, suffragan to Ephesus, a little town on Mount Tmolus's southern slope, facing the Caystrus plain. There people worshipped Artemis Persica, and the town's women were famed for beauty and dancing skill. Its own coinage ran until Emperor Gordianus's time.

Now a little village in the Smyrna region, called Tapou by Turks while Greeks keep the ancient name, it holds classical and medieval ruins. The see lasted until the thirteenth century and under Isaac Angelus Comnenus became metropolitan. Lequien names six bishops, from Mithres at Nicaea in 325 to Gregory at Constantinople in 879, plus Michael, who signed a patriarchal document in 1230.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-santos-a:
Juan Santos Atahualpa was an Indian rebel who shattered Peru's forest missions in 1742. A Cuzco Indian who had served a Jesuit in Spain, he fled to the eastern Andean forests after a murder at Huamanga. There he claimed descent from the Inca chiefs, took the title Atahualpa Apu-Inca, and said God sent him to drive Spain's people from the west of South America.

Able to read and write Latin and Spanish, Santos passed as a powerful wizard among the forest tribes and drew them from Franciscan towns at Ocopa and beyond. His rising ruined the prosperous missions of the Pampa del Sacramento, and Spanish efforts against him failed in the trackless forest. His people still guard his hidden body as a precious fetish.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lampa:
Lampa, or Lappa, was a titular see in Crete, suffragan of Gortyna and probably a colony of Tarrha. Romans stormed it and nearly destroyed it, but Augustus restored it and, for aid against Mark Antony, granted its citizens freedom and the right to coin money.

It is matched with the modern small village of Polis. Its bishopric appears in the Notitiae episcopatuum into the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, and Greeks re-established it near the end of the nineteenth century, with the bishop living at Preveli monastery. Lequien names five bishops. Petrus attended Ephesus in 431, Deneltius Chalcedon in 451, and Prosdocius a council in 458. John appealed to Rome and attended Constantinople in 667, and Epiphanius attended Nicaea in 786.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maestro-di-ca:
The Maestro di Camera del Papa, master of the pope's chamber, is the real chief chamberlain among the palace prelates. Once four in number, major domo, maestro di camera, auditor, and master of the sacred palace, the prelacies shrank. The auditor's post, vacant under Leo XIII, was abolished under Pius X, and the maestro's duties passed to the major domo in 1906.

His authority covers the pope's daily personal service. He commands all chamberlains, clerical and lay, and runs the Anticamera with its four acting privy chamberlains. He tells the Noble, Swiss, and Palace Guards their hours, and summons and dismisses weekly chamberlains. He takes all audience petitions, issues summonses, orders occasional ceremonies such as pilgrimage receptions, and receives each day's orders from the pope himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monomotapa:
Monomotapa was the title of the paramount chief of the Makaranga, a powerful Bantu people. They lived between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers in southern Africa. The word was not the name of an empire. Sixteenth-century Portuguese used it for the ruler, but mapmakers copied it onto their charts as if it marked a vast territory.

From that copying grew a fable. A mighty emperor was said to rule a highly civilised realm from the Zambezi to the Fish River. No such empire existed. The Makaranga realm, called Mokaranga, stood united and strong in the fifteenth century. By the Portuguese arrival in 1505 its chief Makomba had farmed out distant districts to kinsmen who soon broke away. The people remain scattered across Rhodesia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sappa:
Sappa, a diocese in Albania established in 1062 by Alexander II, joined the see of Sarda in 1491 under Innocent VIII. The united sees answered to Antivari until the late eighteenth century. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a small Balkan see through unions and famous bishops.

Sarda itself had absorbed Daynum, founded as an Antivari suffragan in the fourteenth century and joined to Sarda by Martin V in 1428. Sappa's first named bishop is Paulus, about 1370. Its most famous bishops were George Blanko, who from 1623 to 1635 freed his homeland from the Turks, and Lazarus Vladanja of Scutari, who served from 1746 to 1749. The forty-first bishop, James Serecci, suffragan of Scutari, lives at Nensat and rules 17,280 Catholics out of 22,000 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-voluspa:
Völuspá, the Wisdom of the Prophetess, is the most famous mythological poem of the Elder Edda. Telling in vision form the beginning and end of all things and the doom of the gods. The vision belongs to a völva, a wise woman given a role like the Sibyl's in early Christian literature. Odin himself summons her from her grave to answer him, and her prophecy speaks to all men.

Of giant race, her memory reaches back to days when neither earth nor heaven existed, only the yawning chasm, Ginnungagap. The fire giant Surtr gathering, Odin, Thor, and Freyr killed, sun and stars falling, earth sinking into the sea, until a rejuvenated world rises from the ruins.
doe-osti-2999128-probability-density-fun:
Daniel Fletcher, Brian Hehr and Nicholas Asper of Sandia National Laboratories build probability tools for radiation damage, in report SAND2025-12355R, printed October 2025. When a neutron strikes silicon, it knocks atoms out of place and leaves a cluster of defects. In a chip, the size and position of those clusters decide whether a circuit fails. Rather than one average answer, engineers need the odds for where defects land and how hard each hit is.

The team combined three computer models: LAMMPS for atom-level dynamics, plus SRIM and MARLOWE for faster collision tracking. Their probability density functions describe recoil energies and defect patterns, including inside a FinFET transistor shape. Choices inside the models matter: the energy-loss model shifted the averages, while the composition model changed the spread. Multi-channel defects get their own treatment. The report gives device engineers ready distributions for reliability work.
doe-osti-3004707-single-bunch-instabilit:
P. Baxevanis, with A. Blednykh and M. Blaskiewicz, studies a beam problem in Brookhaven technical note BNL-229155-2025-TECH, dated November 2025. The machine is the Electron-Ion Collider's hadron storage ring. At injection, the plan calls for low-energy cooling of the incoming beam. A dense, cold bunch can turn on itself: the particles' own space charge pushes them into collective instabilities.

The note analyzes these single-bunch instabilities under the cooling-at-injection conditions. Space charge effects of this kind are a classic limit in high-intensity rings, treated in literature going back to CERN studies. Knowing the thresholds tells the design team how much current a cooled bunch can safely carry. The work feeds the collider's injection design before hardware is frozen.
doe-osti-3009868-bridging-the-length-sca:
DOE Basic Energy Sciences final report for award DE-SC0022304, from Louisiana State University under principal investigator Revati Kumar with Jose Romagnoli and Christopher Arges of Argonne, covers machine learning for ionic separations. Funding was 1,500,000 dollars across September 2021 to August 2025.

Surrogate models and deep learning connect a membrane material's chemistry and structure to how selectively it moves ions under an electric field. The test mixtures are pH-sensitive, spanning organic acids, silica, boron, and metals such as copper and chromium. A second thread studied bipolar membrane junctions and their water-splitting catalysts for deionization platforms. The tools also spun off an AI framework for designing surfactant molecules.
doe-osti-3010266-real-time-artificial-in:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0021187, by Javier Duarte of UC San Diego, dated December 23, 2025, covers real-time artificial intelligence for the CMS experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The project period ran from September 2020 to August 2025.

The upgraded collider will flood detectors with hundreds of terabytes per second, so events must be judged in less than a microsecond. The team built AI reconstruction algorithms that run on field-programmable gate arrays, using the hls4ml toolchain their community maintains. Physics targets included Higgs bosons produced at large momentum, whose interactions can betray physics beyond the standard model. Benchmarks and surrogate models for estimating chip resources and latency came out of the work.
doe-osti-3013701-liquid-centrifugation-b:
Yuan Yang of Columbia University wrote this final technical report for award DE-SC0024916, covering July 2024 to July 2025, on separating isotopes by spinning liquids. In liquid centrifugation, heavier isotopes drift outward in a spinning solution while lighter ones gather near the axis. The targets here, lithium-7, chlorine-37, and deuterium, all matter to nuclear fission technology.

The report has three parts. The first studies how solute concentration changes separation strength, testing where the Einstein relation between diffusion and mobility holds. The second describes early work building a low-speed countercurrent centrifuge, including a magnetic bearing design damped by an oil bath. The third analyzes candidate chemicals for separating lithium-7 and chlorine-37. The award trained four researchers, from a research scientist to an undergraduate.
doe-osti-3030395-plan-de-acci-n-comunita: Pastillo Tibes got plan-accionado, and this DOE community plan covers energy action. The pages detail the findings. The planners get their data. The plan was community energy. The data were planner. The Tibes were Pastillo. The energy were community.
doe-osti-3031189-testing-of-high-s-matri: DFHLW glass got S-matrix-tested, and this DOE Rev.1 expands composition ranges. The pages detail the high findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The glasses were matrix. The data were nuclear. The 1 were Rev. The ranges were compositional.
doe-osti-3363248-validation-of-a-custom-: Ball-on-ring got custom-validated, and this DOE text considers common issues. The pages detail the apparatus findings. The engineers get their data. The testing was further. The data were engineer. The ring were ball-on. The issues were common.
doe-osti-3484935-energy-storage-technolo: Storage tech got War-requiremented, and this DOE text covers Department of War needs. The pages detail the technologies findings. The energy folks get their data. The requirements were US. The data were energy. The War were Department. The storage were technologies.
doe-osti-3625658-design-of-a-cryogenic-a: Quantum computers live at near absolute zero — and stray infrared light can wreck their qubits. Mailliard and Temples built a deep-cold test rig for comparing how different qubit packages leak infrared. The head-to-head points to packaging that keeps qubits cold and quiet.
govdocs-archive_org-PhysicalControlOfThe:
José M. R. Delgado was a Spanish-born brain researcher at Yale who spent his career testing whether behavior could be steered by electrical signals sent straight into the brain. His 1969 book sums up that work and argues that people stand close to a new age of control over their own minds.

Delgado describes his stimoceiver, a small radio device implanted in the brain that could trigger movements and moods at the push of a button. His best-known test stopped a charging bull in a ring with a radio signal. He closes by urging society to use such tools for mental liberation rather than fear them, a claim still argued over today.
govdocs-archive_org-TheFirstHolocaust-Je:
Don Heddesheimer wrote The First Holocaust as volume 6 of the Barnes Review's Holocaust Handbook Series. His subject is World War I-era Jewish fund-raising campaigns in America and the claims made in them about Jewish suffering in Europe.

Heddesheimer points to reports such as a 1919 New York Times item speaking of six million Jews, and argues that such figures were raised for fund-raising effect long before World War II. The book is revisionist history and is widely disputed by historians. It is held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers studying that literature itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Preparation-Ear:
An editorial asks whether Watergate is ending, under the line 'Watergate: An End Is in Sight?' Its subject is Leon Jaworski, the special prosecutor. Jaworski was struggling to obtain 64 White House tapes from President Nixon. Nixon, for his part, was working to bring the scandal to an end on his own terms.

The tapes fight decided Watergate. A prosecutor subpoenaed recordings; a president claimed privilege; the courts would settle it. An editorial of that season shows how the struggle looked before the settlement: uncertain, procedural, and political at once. The piece preserves the press taking the nation's temperature mid-crisis, when the outcome that now seems fixed was still in doubt.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico-a:
In September 2014, forty-three students from the Ayotzinapa teachers' college in Mexico vanished after attacks in Iguala. Kate Doyle and Claire Dorfman edited this briefing book, number 823, published in March 2023. It draws on the Guacamaya leaks, a large trove of hacked military files.

The leaks show Mexico's military had surveilled the Ayotzinapa school for years before the disappearance. Intelligence reports reveal a constant exchange of messages during the night of the attacks themselves. Yet the military continues to deny investigators complete access to its archives. The posting joins leaked proof of watching with official refusal to open the rest.
lippa:
Beatrice Kemp, writing as Beatrice Egerton, published this novel in London. Eden, Remington and Company issued it from King Street, Covent Garden. Chapter One opens at four o'clock on a deserted July street. Cab-drivers sleep while sentries swelter in their bearskins.

Jimmy Dalrymple confesses to his friend Chubby that he is nearly done. Heat and money troubles press on the young Guards officer. Chubby blames racing, and Jimmy calls him an ass. A Shakespeare epigraph frames life as a stage for every man. Jimmy serves in the Guards, readers learn from the club talk. Helmdon, better known as Chubby, lectures him on racing habits.
nasa-tm-19710011026-an-improved-method-f:
Charles L Zola of the Lewis Research Center published this method in February 1971. It tackles a payload problem for spacecraft that use electric propulsion at low power levels. Fitting less than the best power level can cut payload sharply. Zola asked whether a lighter spacecraft could recover some of that loss.

His answer was yes. For a given launcher, the best total spacecraft mass can sit below the most mass the launcher can inject. Trimming mass raises the payload share when electric power is scarce. Zola showed the method on a Mercury orbiter design. It used solar electric propulsion and a Titan Centaur launcher.
nasa-tm-19710019493-materials-technology:
R E Gluyas and A F Lietzke of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a June 1971 nuclear meeting in Boston. It lays out a materials program for a compact fast reactor meant to supply power in space. The fuel was uranium mononitride, clad in a tantalum alloy with a tungsten liner. Every material had to survive hot liquid lithium coolant.

One half of the program developed the factory process. It covers making the fuel, cladding, and finished fuel pins, plus inspection. The other half ran compatibility studies. Fuel had to suit its cladding and the coolant. The team also checked control drum and reflector materials. The goal was a fuel element ready for reactor service.
nasa-tm-19720020704-results-of-the-ballo:
The Goddard Space Flight Center issued these experiment results in March 1972, numbered X-524-72-125. The Balloon Atmospheric Propagation Experiment flew its first flights in 1970. Two laser beams climbed from the ground to receivers carried above most of the air. One beam was green argon light, and the other was infrared. Earth's atmosphere makes such beams twinkle and waver. The flights measured that shimmering, called scintillation, directly.

At the same time, instruments tracked the turbulence along the path. Matching the two records showed how air motion distorts laser light. Balloons lifted the receivers clear of the thickest air. The work served designers of laser links between ground and space. Its short name was BAPE 1, marking the first flight series.
podcast-tuckercarlson-aLtfKq08YpA:
Tucker Carlson gives a talk on the spiritual roots of America's political breakdown. He argues the crisis in public life is at base a crisis of faith. No guest joins him, so the episode is his case alone, made at length.

Carlson says a country that loses shared belief in God loses shared truth as well. He links that loss to rage in politics, broken homes, and a sense of drift. He also takes aim at leaders who mock faith while the country frays. Listeners get his full frame for the age in one place. Fans and critics alike can hear the claim as he states it.
the-curlytops-on-star-island-or-camping-: Howard R. Garis wrote The Curlytops on Star Island, or Camping Out with Grandpa, with pictures by Julia Greene. A series page dated 1918 lists the Curlytops books: At Cherry Farm, On Star Island, Snowed In, and At Uncle Frank's Ranch. The contents open with chapters called The Blue Light, What the Farmer Told, Off to Star Island, Overboard, The Bag of Salt, and Ted and the Bear. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here.
the-fotygraft-album-shown-to-the-new-nei:
Frank Wing drew and wrote The Fotygraft Album, shown to a new neighbor by Rebecca Sparks Peters, aged eleven. The book was printed at Chicago in 1915 and ran through seven printings in a year.

Rebecca greets Mrs. Miggs at the door while her mother is out borrowing thread, molasses, and eggs. She sits the guest down and turns the album pages, one kin folk at a time. Her mother as a girl wears real mink from Uncle Seth's store. Aunt Mary Jane is praised for jimpson-weed salve and peach preserves. Each photo brings a child's plain talk on kin, looks, and worth.
tom-swift-and-his-motor-boat-or-the-riva:
Victor Appleton opens with Mr. Barton Swift asking his son where he is going, as Tom pushes his motor-cycle toward the country road. Tom plainly has an object in view. Contents promise twenty-five chapters beginning at a motor-boat auction on Lake Carlopa, with lively bidding and a timely warning.

Tom and Andy clash repeatedly, the Arrow disappears, robbery news arrives, and a balloon catches fire before a rescue. Plans for an airship and a solved mystery lead to winning a race. Readers get an early Tom Swift adventure built around speed, rivals, and a father's watchful questions.
